passage: I'm Sarita, Mahima's cousin. Mahima is five and her birthday is on Saturday. She keeps asking, "Is it tomorrow?" Every night we count sleeps on her fingers. On Thursday she said, "Yesterday was three sleeps, today is two, tomorrow is one!" She still hops around impatiently, but she stops asking every hour. I'm not sure she understands weeks yet, but she gets sleeps.

qa.q: When is Mahima's birthday?
qa.a: Her birthday is on Saturday.

qa.q: What does Mahima's hopping around suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she was excited and finding it hard to wait.

qa.q: What helped Mahima understand the days?
qa.a: Counting sleeps on her fingers each night helped her track yesterday, today and tomorrow.

qa.q: How does Sarita see Mahima's understanding of time?
qa.a: She thinks Mahima understands sleeps but maybe not weeks yet.

grounding: An older cousin observes a child learning the sequence of days and waiting.

"Yesterday we packed. Today we ride the train. Tomorrow morning we wake at Nani's."

Darshan, five, crossed off another box on the kitchen calendar in their Indore home with a red crayon. "Is it Asif's party today?"

"Not today," Ammi said. "Tomorrow."

Darshan groaned. "Tomorrow is too long."

"Yesterday you went to the park, right? Today you have school. Then sleep. Then party."

Darshan counted on his fingers: park, school, sleep, party. "Okay. Only one sleep."

He put the crayon down and went back to building a tower while he waited.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel about waiting for the party?
qa.a: He felt impatient, groaning that tomorrow was too long.

qa.q: How might Asif feel if he knew Darshan was counting the days?
qa.a: Asif would probably feel happy that a friend is so excited about the party.

grounding: Shows a young child using a calendar and events to understand yesterday, today and tomorrow while waiting.

passage:
"Is it tomorrow now?" Raghav, five, asked, climbing onto the bed.

"No, it's today," Sabina Aunty said. "Nani comes tomorrow."

"But yesterday you said tomorrow!"

"Yes. Yesterday, tomorrow was today. Now tomorrow is the next day."

Raghav scrunched his face. "That's confusing."

"It is. Look, when you wake up after one sleep, Nani will be here."

He lay down and closed his eyes tight. "I'm sleeping fast."

Sabina Aunty laughed. "Sleeping fast doesn't work. But try."

qa.q: Who is coming tomorrow?
qa.a: Nani is coming tomorrow.

qa.q: Why did Raghav close his eyes tight and say he was sleeping fast?
qa.a: He was so eager to see Nani that he hoped sleeping quickly would bring tomorrow sooner.

qa.q: What made Sabina Aunty's "one sleep" explanation useful?
qa.a: It gave Raghav a concrete way to measure time that fits how young children understand days.

qa.q: What would change if Sabina Aunty got impatient with his questions?
qa.a: Raghav might feel more confused and upset, instead of feeling it is okay to find time tricky 🙂

grounding: A dialogue shows a young child working out yesterday, today and tomorrow while waiting for a visit.

passage:
Class note. Teacher: Sabina.
Nikita (five) asked me six times today, “Is it my birthday?” Her birthday is on Friday.
So I made a paper chain with three links. “Each morning, you tear one link. When there are no links, it's your birthday.”
She tore one today. “Yesterday I had four sleeps. Today three. Tomorrow two!” she said.
She didn't ask again all afternoon.
Next step: I'll use paper chains for the class trip next month.

qa.q: How many times did Nikita ask if it was her birthday?
qa.a: She asked six times today.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel about waiting for her birthday?
qa.a: She felt impatient and excited, asking again and again.

qa.q: Why did the paper chain help Nikita wait?
qa.a: It showed her the days in a way she could see and count, so waiting felt easier.

qa.q: How might the teacher feel when Nikita stops asking?
qa.a: The teacher probably feels relieved and pleased that the chain helped.

grounding: A teacher helps a five-year-old understand days until her birthday and wait calmly.

passage:
In their village near Amritsar, Gurleen, five, stood at the gate every evening. “Is Papa coming today?”
“Not today,” said Vandana. “The day after tomorrow.”
“Is that far?”
Vandana gave her two pebbles. “Throw one in the pot tonight, and one tomorrow night. Then Papa comes.”
That night Gurleen threw one. “Tomorrow, one more. Then Papa!”
She stopped waiting at the gate and went to feed the calf.

qa.q: How many pebbles did Vandana give Gurleen?
qa.a: She gave her two pebbles.

qa.q: How was Gurleen feeling as she stood at the gate each evening?
qa.a: She felt impatient and missed her Papa.

qa.q: What did Vandana do that helped Gurleen understand?
qa.a: She used pebbles to show the days, so Gurleen could see how long to wait.

qa.q: How might Papa feel when he arrives and sees Gurleen?
qa.a: He probably feels happy and loved, knowing she counted the days.

grounding: A five-year-old learns to count the days until her father returns and waits more calmly.

passage:
In Prague, Tomas, five, woke up and asked Clara, “Is Babička coming today?”
Clara pointed to the calendar on the fridge. “Yesterday was Friday. Today is Saturday. Babička comes tomorrow, Sunday.”
Tomas looked at the calendar. He touched Friday, then Saturday, then Sunday.
“So one more sleep?”
“One more sleep.”
He sighed. “That's long.”
“Shall we bake her a cake today, so it's ready tomorrow?”
Tomas jumped up. “Yes!”

qa.q: When does Babička come?
qa.a: She comes tomorrow, Sunday.

qa.q: How did Tomas feel about waiting one more sleep?
qa.a: He felt impatient, sighing that it was long.

qa.q: How did Clara help Tomas with waiting?
qa.a: She showed him the days on the calendar and gave him a fun task for today.

qa.q: How might Babička feel when she sees the cake?
qa.a: She would probably feel happy and loved that Tomas prepared for her visit.

grounding: A five-year-old learns the order of days and waits for his grandmother's visit.

passage:
I'm Vikas, from the flat below. In the last days of Ramadan, Ayesha kept asking her mother, "Is it Eid today?"
Her mother drew a row of moons on a paper and stuck it on the fridge. Every morning Ayesha crossed one out.
On the fourth morning, I heard her count. "Three moons left. So not today. Not tomorrow." She pouted, but she didn't cry like before.
On Eid morning she banged on our door in her new dress. "No more moons!"

qa.q: Where did Ayesha's mother stick the paper of moons?
qa.a: On the fridge.

qa.q: What does Ayesha's pout on the fourth morning suggest?
qa.a: Ayesha still felt impatient, but she was learning to wait without getting as upset.

qa.q: How could Ayesha's mother use the same idea for other waits?
qa.a: She could make a similar chart for a birthday or a trip, so Ayesha can see the days left.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel when Ayesha bangs on the door on Eid morning?
qa.a: Vikas probably feels amused and happy to share her excitement.

grounding: A neighbour watches a young child count down the days to Eid on a chart.

passage:
Two weeks before Diwali, Arohi asked every day, "Is Ayesha didi coming today?" Each time the answer was "Not yet," and she cried.
Her father made a paper chain with fourteen loops. "Tear one every night after dinner."
One week in, Arohi tore a loop and counted the rest. "Seven. That's lots of sleeps." She looked sad, but she went to bed.
On Diwali eve, she tore the last one and ran to the gate. Ayesha stepped out of the auto, and Arohi jumped into her arms.

qa.q: How many loops did the paper chain have?
qa.a: Fourteen loops.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when she counted seven loops left?
qa.a: Arohi felt sad that the wait was still long, but she accepted it and went to bed.

qa.q: Why did the paper chain help Arohi wait?
qa.a: It turned the days into something she could see and tear, so "not yet" became a number that got smaller.

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel when Arohi jumps into her arms?
qa.a: Ayesha would likely feel loved and happy ❤️ that Arohi had been waiting for her.

grounding: Over two weeks before Diwali a child learns to wait for a cousin's visit using a paper chain.

passage:
During the monsoon, Sudha, five, kept asking her grandmother Nazia, "Is it my birthday now?"
"Not today. Tomorrow."
Then the storm knocked out the power, and the cake shop closed early. Sudha cried. "Then it's never!"
Nazia lit a candle. "Today is the storm. Tomorrow is your birthday. We'll bake a cake together tomorrow."
Sudha counted on her fingers. "Today. Then sleep. Then tomorrow."
She went to bed early to make tomorrow come faster.

qa.q: When is Sudha's birthday?
qa.a: Tomorrow.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel when the cake shop closed?
qa.a: She felt upset and disappointed, crying that it would never come.

qa.q: How did Nazia help Sudha understand the wait?
qa.a: She explained today and tomorrow clearly and promised a plan to bake a cake together.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel when Sudha goes to bed early?
qa.a: Nazia likely feels amused and fond.

grounding: Shows a young child learning today and tomorrow and tolerating waiting despite a setback.

"No. Tomorrow."

passage:
Note from Nani, Rakhi week.
Hrithik, four, asked every hour, "Is Arohi didi coming today?" I drew three boxes on the fridge: yesterday, today, tomorrow. Yesterday he tied a paper rakhi on his teddy. Today we bought sweets. Tomorrow, Arohi comes.
At bedtime he said, "Tomorrow is after sleeping, na?" and ran to bed early.
This morning he crossed out "today" himself and shouted, "Now it's Arohi day!" He waited at the window for an hour, only fidgeting a little.
Next: I'll use the boxes for his birthday countdown.

qa.q: What did Hrithik tie a paper rakhi on yesterday?
qa.a: He tied a paper rakhi on his teddy.

qa.q: What does Hrithik running to bed early suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he felt excited and hopeful, understanding that sleeping would bring tomorrow and his sister sooner. 😊

qa.q: How did Nani help Hrithik understand yesterday, today and tomorrow?
qa.a: She drew three boxes on the fridge and linked each day to something real, so he could see and mark time passing.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel when she hears Hrithik waited at the window?
qa.a: Arohi would probably feel touched and loved, knowing her little brother counted the days until she came.

grounding: Shows a young child learning the order of days and managing to wait.
